description:
I'm Mohammad, a Palestinian student interested in AI, robotics, and space exploration. My skills include programming, AI tools, and turning ideas into working prototypes.

PIONEER X is a solo team working on the Martian Map challenge: a simple, clear navigation tool built on real NASA data that any astronaut can understand in seconds.

I'm not recruiting at the moment, but happy to connect and exchange ideas at the Ramallah event, Nov 14–15.
summary: MARSWAY turns a real NASA rover campaign into a survival guide for the first people to walk on Mars. From May 2025 to February 2026, Curiosity spent 272 sols exploring the "boxwork" ridges of Mount Sharp, Gale crater, and stopped at 65 science sites. MARSWAY replays that campaign as 12 crewed, two-person Marswalks. It plans every walk over real terrain using the USGS 1 m elevation model and least-cost routes that avoid unsafe slopes. It budgets oxygen and suit power, shows the point of no return, and tracks radiation (Curiosity RAD), weather (REMS) and space weather (NASA DONKI). It answers two planning questions with numbers. First, where to build the base: every 20 m of the area was tested, and the best site cuts walking time by 54%. Second, what to do when reality departs from the plan: a live decision engine re-plans the EVA after delays, heavy workload, rover failure or radiation alerts. Every number carries a measured, derived or estimated label with its source.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

MARSWAY turns a real NASA rover campaign into a survival guide for the first people to walk on Mars. From May 2025 to February 2026, Curiosity spent 272 sols exploring the "boxwork" ridges of Mount Sharp, Gale crater, and stopped at 65 science sites. MARSWAY replays that campaign as crewed Marswalks:

- Mission Control: 12 two-person EVAs built from Curiosity's 65 real science stops.

- Mission brief: objective, route, distance, EVA time, risks, oxygen and suit battery. It compares four route options: fastest, shortest, safest, and Curiosity's own track. Crew roles are EV1 and EV2, with an optional unpressurised rover. A walkback check shows that the crew can still walk home in time if the rover fails.

- Animated Mission Guide: walks the crew through each site along the real elevation profile. The hands-on task at each stop is chosen from what Curiosity's instruments actually did there.

- Navigation: step-by-step instructions and a life-support HUD (EVA time, O2, battery, radiation, terrain, weather, daylight). It shows Curiosity's real raw images of each site and has a tap-anywhere point-of-no-return check. Voice guidance is available in English or Arabic.

- Live decision support: the EVA re-plans itself after a delay, heavy workload, a rover failure or a radiation alert. It decides which sites to keep (documented drill sites first), which to drop, or when to return now, using the time and oxygen actually left. Every decision is logged.

- Base planner: where should the habitat be? Every 20 m cell of the 2 x 2 km area is tested as a base site, using the slope limits applied to Curiosity's own landing site. A base at the rover's start point needs 12 EVAs and 59.8 h. The best site needs 11 EVAs and 53.9 h, with 54% less walking.

- Printable cuff checklist in the Apollo style, and a mission journal with photos.

- Science Lab: a replay of Curiosity's campaign, a Marswalk planner, 12 NASA Mars Trek layers from 6 missions, and a space-weather timeline. On the timeline, rises in RAD dose are cross-checked with NASA DONKI events.

HOW IT WORKS

A 14-step Python pipeline turns NASA and USGS data into static files that the app reads:

- Terrain and routes: a window of the USGS 1 m elevation model of Gale crater is processed to get slope and roughness. A walking-cost surface uses a Tobler-type walking model with a suit factor derived from Apollo data. Least-cost routes are found with scikit-image. Stops are grouped into EVAs that fit an 8-hour EVA with a 30% reserve.

- Radiation: Curiosity RAD dose for all 272 campaign sols, read from the NASA PDS archive.

- Consumables: oxygen from Apollo metabolic rates, and suit battery from EMU battery data.

- Weather and space weather: Curiosity REMS daily weather and NASA DONKI events.

- Base siting: 65 least-cost fields are used to evaluate 10,000 candidate sites.

The website is plain HTML/JavaScript with Leaflet and has no backend. Progress and the journal stay in the browser. An Android app (APK) wraps the same site with a phone layout, native text-to-speech and printing. 47 automated tests check the data.

BENEFITS AND INTENDED IMPACT

- It plans human EVAs on real Mars terrain, against real science targets, in real conditions.

- It shows what a crew could add to a rover campaign.

- It turns two key mission-design questions into numbers: where to build the base, and how to survive the unplanned.

- Our goal is a field-ready planning and decision tool that can start from any landing site with NASA data, and that trains crews to make go / no-go decisions before they leave Earth.

TOOLS, LANGUAGES AND SOFTWARE

- Pipeline: Python (rasterio/GDAL, NumPy, SciPy, scikit-image, Shapely, Pillow, PyYAML, requests, pytest).

- Web: JavaScript, HTML/CSS, Leaflet 1.9.4.

- Android: Java with AndroidX WebKit.

- Documents: ReportLab, svglib, matplotlib and headless Chrome.

- AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic), as disclosed in the app and the documents.

No special hardware was used.

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

Instead of an imaginary route, MARSWAY replays a real rover campaign as if astronauts had done it. The science targets, images, radiation and weather are what Curiosity actually met. The app does more than show a map. It answers questions a mission planner must answer, and it re-plans live when things go wrong. The interface works like a field tool: a HUD, a cuff checklist, voice guidance and an Arabic interface.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Safety first: oxygen and battery reserves, a point of no return, walking back if the rover fails, radiation alerts, and slope limits.

- Honesty about data: every number is labelled measured, derived or estimated, with its source. Values without a published source are labelled as assumptions.

- Usability: an astronaut must understand each screen in seconds, it works offline as a static site, and it works on phones (Android APK).

- Accessibility: English and Arabic, voice guidance, and a reduced-motion option.
